content: The country or another country may have programs in place through existing agreements, supported by sustainable national funding. Examples include Field Epidemiology Training Programs, International Health Regulations, and public health workforce initiatives. Data reporting for these programs occurs every three years, with potential data sources such as the Ministry of Health, public health institutions, and educational and training institutions. The governance indicators assess whether a country can coordinate an intersectoral health workforce agenda and has a central health workforce unit. Health workforce policy indicators evaluate whether the country has processes for workforce planning, whether education plans align with the national health plan, and whether institutional models exist to assess healthcare staffing needs. Governance indicators include mechanisms to coordinate intersectoral health workforce agendas and the presence of a central health workforce unit. Health workforce policy indicators include planning processes, alignment of education plans with national health plans, and institutional models for assessing staffing needs. For governance, mechanisms may include national coordination committees, interministerial Sustainable Development Goals committees, or sector skills councils. These bodies should coordinate, develop, and monitor health workforce policies and plans while negotiating intersectoral relationships with other ministries, government agencies, and stakeholders. Key questions for governance include: 1. Is there a coordinating mechanism or body in place? 2. Are various stakeholders involved in the coordination process? 3. Has an agenda been formulated and approved at the interministerial level? For health workforce planning, indicators assess whether clear objectives are set in national health policies, whether communication and information flow among stakeholders are coordinated, and whether a dedicated Human Resources for Health Planning Committee exists. They also evaluate whether a methodology for workforce planning is established, whether complete data for quantitative assessments are available, and whether policy actions based on committee recommendations are implemented. Education plans should align with national health plans and address health worker competencies, population needs, health systems, and labor market demands. Plans should consider transformative education and training efforts, and recognized institutions should offer training on implementing and monitoring health policies. Strategic steps should account for workforce market needs and absorptive capacities. Institutional models for assessing staffing needs should include mechanisms to determine the required number of health workers for effective and safe service delivery and to assess workload in health facilities. Human Resource for Health Information Systems (HRHIS) should support international reporting, including on International Health Regulations (IHR), the WHO Code of Practice, and skilled attendance at birth. HRHIS should also track health workforce flows and stocks, including outputs from education and training institutions, labor market entrants, active workforce stock, and exits from the labor market. It should produce geocoded locations of health facilities. Key questions for HRHIS include: 1. Is there a master list of accredited education and training institutions at the national level? 2. Is this list geocoded and regularly updated? 3. Do institutions record the number of graduates by health workforce education and training, disaggregated by sex? 4. Is information on graduates provided to relevant national bodies annually? Data reporting for HRHIS occurs annually, with potential sources including the Ministry of Health, professional chambers, and national statistical offices.
